writingIdeas.viewpoint: Stable renting should be a realistic long-term option.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Tenants need reasonable security if renting is to function as a genuine form of housing.
writingIdeas.argument: Short contracts can force families to move even when they have paid rent reliably. Frequent moves disrupt children’s schooling, commuting arrangements and neighbourhood ties. Clear rules on notice periods and reasonable rent increases would give tenants more stability. Landlords would retain the right to manage their property and address serious breaches. A fair rental system should balance ownership rights with the need for a secure home.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: New housing should be built near transport and services.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Location is as important as the number of homes constructed.
writingIdeas.argument: Cheap land on the edge of a city may allow rapid construction, but residents can face long and costly journeys. Housing near employment, schools and frequent transport gives people more practical choices. It also reduces pressure to own a car and can support local shops. Planning authorities should coordinate housing with infrastructure rather than treating them as separate projects. A home is affordable only when the cost of reaching daily needs is considered.

speaking.question: What is your favourite room in your home?
speaking.answer: My favourite room is the small study near the window. It isn’t beautifully decorated, but it gets good natural light and is quieter than the rest of the flat. I use it for reading and work, and I keep the desk fairly clear. Having one place associated with concentration helps me settle down quickly.

speaking.question: What would you like to change about your home?
speaking.answer: I’d improve the storage. The flat itself is large enough, but there aren’t many cupboards, so everyday objects easily make the rooms look untidy. Built-in shelves would use the vertical space without taking up much floor area. I’d also replace one harsh ceiling light with several warmer lamps, which would make the living room more comfortable.

reading.title: The Flexible Rooms of the Past
paragraphs: Modern property advertisements usually name each room: bedroom, dining room, study and living room. The label suggests a fixed purpose. In many earlier homes, however, rooms changed function throughout the day. Furniture was moved, beds were folded or shared, and the same space might be used for work, meals and sleep. Limited space made flexibility ordinary rather than fashionable.

Industrialisation gradually altered this pattern for many urban households. Work moved from homes into factories and offices, while mass-produced furniture became cheaper. Rising incomes allowed some families to separate private sleeping areas from spaces used for guests. These changes were uneven; overcrowded housing continued, and domestic workers often occupied rooms with several functions.

Flexible design has returned in response to smaller apartments and remote work. Sliding partitions, folding tables and movable storage allow residents to change a room without increasing its size. Yet flexibility has limits. A worker who packs away a desk every evening may never gain a quiet place for concentration, and family members can compete for the same adaptable space at the same time.

Housing quality therefore cannot be measured by floor area alone. Layout, daylight, sound and storage affect whether space can genuinely serve several purposes. A smaller home with well-positioned doors and adequate cupboards may function better than a larger one divided into awkward rooms. Flexibility is most useful when it expands choice; it is less convincing when it merely gives a positive name to insufficient space.

Household composition makes flexible space more complicated. A studio may suit one resident but become difficult when two people work from home or a child needs quiet sleep. Designers cannot predict every future arrangement, yet sufficient electrical points, sound separation and storage allow residents to adapt later without major rebuilding. Adaptability begins with practical capacity, not movable furniture alone.
